AGENDA
  BLUE RIBBON PENSION REVIEW COMMITTEE
  VIA TELECONFERENCE ONLY
 Meetings are broadcast live on Glendale TV, viewable on Spectrum Cable, channel 6, and AT&T U-
 verse, channel 99. Meetings are also streamed live in high definition (HD) on the city's webpage,
 glendaleca.gov/live, on YouTube.com/myglendale, and on Apple TV, Roku, and Amazon Fire devices
 using a free app called Screenweave and choosing “Glendale TV” from the menu. Meetings are also
 archived on the City Website for viewing anytime at glendaleca.gov/agendas. Call (818) 548-4013 for
 program schedules. DVDs of the proceedings are available for purchase in the City Clerk's Office.
 If you have any question about matters on the agenda, or requests for assistance, please contact the
 Management Services Department at (818) 548-4844, during regular business hours.
  PLEASE TURN OFF CELLULAR PHONES WHILE INSIDE THE MEETING LOCATION
 In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990, auxiliary hearing aids, sign
 language translation, and Braille transcripts are available upon request. Assisted listening devices
 are available same-day upon request. At least 48 hours (or two business days) notice is required for
 requests regarding sign language translation and Braille transcription services. All documents related
 to open session items on this agenda that are received less than 72 hours prior to this meeting, and
 are public records, will be available for review in the Office of the City Clerk, 613 E. Broadway, RM
 110, Glendale, CA 91206.
 Translation services are provided for meetings through the use of bilingual staff for speakers who
 wish to utilize the service as available. Speakers should state their request by contacting the City
 Clerk’s office at (818) 548-2090, at least 24 hours prior to the scheduled meeting. Please specify
 the language for which you require translation. The exclusive use of City provided interpreters is not
 required and persons are welcome to use their own interpreter or speak in their native language.
  OCTOBER 18, 2021 AT 6:30 PM

To help slow the transmission of COVID-19, and protect the health and safety of the community, City
Council, as well as Board & Commission meetings, will continue to be closed to the public for in-person
attendance.
The public is encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes to practice social
distancing. Meetings are broadcast live on Glendale TV, viewable on Spectrum Cable, channel 6, and
AT&T U-verse, channel 99. Meetings are also streamed live in high definition (HD) on the city's webpage,
glendaleca.gov/live, on YouTube.com/myglendale, and on Apple TV, Roku, and Amazon Fire devices
using a free app called Screenweave and choosing “Glendale TV” from the menu.
For public comments and questions during the meeting, call (818) 937-8100. Public comments on a
specific agenda item will be taken when that agenda item is discussed.

CITY OF GLENDALE
  BLUE RIBBON PENSION REVIEW COMMITTEE
  REGULAR MEETING MINUTES

  October 18, 2021

ROLL CALL

Meeting began at 6:34pm

Present: Finch, Manning, Michals, Palos, Wenz, Kedikian, Amirian, Molano, Wolfson,
Zakarian

Absent: Bain, Knights, Masias, Nelson, IBEW rep

Staff: Doyle, Takhtalian, Flynn, Garcia, Hovsepian, Bradford, Cerritos, Jensen,
Holtzman, Soghomonyan, Ross

  1. REGULAR BUSINESS AGENDA
  a. Report of Recorder, re: Posting of Agenda. Mr. Soghomonyan reports that
  the Agenda for the October 18, 2021 Blue Ribbon Pension Review
  Committee was Posted on October 15, 2021, on the Bulletin Board
  Outside City Hall.

  2. ORAL COMMUNICATIONS
  None

  3. MINUTES
  a. Approval of the minutes of the Special Meeting on September 29,
  2021

Amirian asks if the start time for this meeting is correct about the timing for the first
session. Jensen answers in the affirmative.

  b. Approval of the minutes of the Regular Meeting on October 4, 2021

Kedikian moves to approve the minutes for a) and b).
Wolfson seconds.

Aye: Amirian, Kedikian, Manning, Masias, Michals, Molano, Wolfson, Finch, Wenz,
Zakarian, Palos
Noes:
Abstain

  1
 Motion passes.

  c. Approval of the minutes of the Special Meeting of the Executive
  Committee on October 11, 2021.

c) will be up for approval at the next Executive Committee meeting.

  4. BUSINESS ITEMS

  a. Q&A Regarding City Staff’s Presentation from October 4, 2021, about
  City Pension Obligations

Holtzman notes that Molano sent a list of questions, some which are not directly related
to the Staff’s presentation. Holtzman announces that he will be asking folks in
alphabetical order to ask questions of Staff.

Holtzman calls on Amirian.
Amirian has no questions.

Holtzman calls on Finch.
Finch has no questions.

Holtzman calls on Kedikian
Kedikian asks about what the City has done to deal with impacts on CalPERs changes
to benefits. He asks if the City has investigated whether CalPERS breached fiduciary
duties, and whether the City can sue CalPERS for mismanagement. He also asks
whether the City sought a legal opinion on CalPERS changes in 2001. He would like to
know what the City has not done to deal with its pension obligations.

Holtzman asks if Flynn was in the City in 2001.
Flynn answers that she was an internal auditor at the time. Holtzman asks if she was
involved at the time. Flynn does not recall being directly involved in it at all. Doyle notes
that he was a staff member in HR at the time. He explains that CalPERS reports in 2001
held that the City was super-funded, which lead to the enhanced benefit plans and cities
increasing their benefits in competition with each other. He adds that there was a
tremendous amount of pressure, that California was dealing with the .com bubble, that
the economy was doing very well, and that this led to increases everywhere. Glendale
was unique in requiring that employees take some of the cost share of employee and
employer share. Doyle believes that all retirement enhancements as they affected
police and fire were only implemented when those organizations agreed to pay some of
the employer’s share of CalPERS which was not common then.

  2
 Holtzman adds that from a legal position, these were labor negotiations. He notes that
one of the major costs of going to 3%@50 is that people were credited for their work at
that rate going all the way back to their start date. What employees contributed earlier
was a lower rate than what could fund the new rate, which created unfunded liability.

Molano asks to respond to Doyle’s comments.
Holtzman requests that Molano wait until giving others the opportunity to ask questions.

Holtzman calls on Manning.
Manning has no questions.

Holtzman calls on Masias.
Masias has no questions.

Holtzman calls on Michals.
Michals has no questions.

Holtzman calls on Molano.
Molano asks: what is the highest sum the City has paid to CalPERS in any one year?
Flynn notes that she would have to check to make sure, but she believes that the
largest sum is from this year.

Molano states that having an employee pay into the employer’s cost share is really
having the employee paying into their own benefit, and, if at the same time, that
employee receives a wage increase at a rate higher than the rate of inflation, then the
City is essentially paying the employee to pay for his benefits. He adds that when the
City decided in 2001 to enhance benefits, they were looking at financial records from
previous years, e.g. year 2000 in the CAFR, which had the assets of CalPERS based
on 1999, and which was one of the richest years of the .com bubble. But by the time the
City made the decision in 2001, there was an implosion in the stock market and a
recession; when Council decided to enhance benefits, 100s of millions of dollars were
already lost. Molano notes that if the Council was misinformed or misled in the
information they received, and if the City made a change at Staff request, then they may
have based their decision on the basis of bad information.

Holtzman calls on Palos.
Palos has no questions.

Holtzman calls on Wenz.
Wenz has no questions.

Holtzman calls on Wolfson.

  3
 Wolfson asks about portion of presentation related to page 6 of 2015 Staff report, noting
a discrepancy in the contribution rates.
Holtzman asks Takhtalian to go back and figure out an explanation to the issue before
the next session. Takhtalian notes that he will go back to staff who put the presentation
together and get an answer for Wolfson.

Holtzman calls on Zakarian.
Zakarian has no questions at this time.

Holtzman asks the Committee about the extent to which they want to focus on past
mistakes vs. where we are currently and what the possible solutions are. Holtzman
notes that his understanding of the Committee’s purpose was to focus on the later. He
suggests that the Committee reflect on this as it goes forward. Molano comments that
when a sick man goes to the doctor with several problems, the doctor will ask about
what he’s done in the past; the doctor looks at the patient’s history to determine what
condition the person is in currently.

  b. Presentation from Linda Ross about Vesting Rights

Holtzman introduces Linda Ross’s presentation on vesting rights. Linda introduces
herself, noting that she has litigated the last three big cases on vesting rights.

Ross presents on the following topics:
   History of the “California Rule:
   Limits on the California Rules
   Relevant recent California Supreme Court decisions
   Good news as a result of those decisions vis-à-vis pension reform
   The future of pension reform

Holtzman notes that changes to prospective benefits will require legislative changes and
for the Supreme Court to decide on issues that it has not weighed in on yet, so we are
far from knowing whether we can fundamentally change the pension formula

Manning asks if there are any significant cases in the pipeline?
Ross answers that there are not any to her knowledge.
Holtzman asks about San Diego’s initiative regarding their independent retirement
system.

Zakarain notes that proposition B from San Diego was overruled and dismissed.
Holtzman notes that PERB struck down the measure on the grounds that they had
failed to meet and confer on the measure. He adds that the measure was independent
and didn’t, on the face of it, require meet and confer.

  4
 Wolfson asks whether anyone on the Committee has suggested that we undo any one’s
vested rights?
Holtzman notes that he doesn’t think anyone has made any suggestions on the topic
either way, but that the point of the presentation is to give guidelines on the changes
that may be made and may not be made.

Kedikian asks for future presentations to be provided ahead of time.
Holtzman notes that he and Staff will try their best to do so in the future.

Molano asks if a City separate from CalPERS, and without legislation, create a
compensation cap for employees hired after 2013.
Holtzman responds that he believes the answer is no because he thinks CalPERS
would take the position that it would insist on its money for everything that falls within its
definition of final compensation and will base pension on that.
Ross adds that she believes it was confirmed in the Alameda case that pension is a
creature of state law, but that there are some cases where State law permits changes
through collective bargaining.

Zakarian asks about how the 80% funded liability is calculated and what it reflects.
Ross answers that it’s an actuarial calculation: actuaries take all retirees and employees
in the pipeline and ask (i) what the total liability is that they will have to pay over time
and (ii) do we have enough money on hand to pay that. That’s where they come up with
the 80%. She adds that in 2000, CalPERS was flush with money and that was one
basis upon which a lot of employers granted enhanced pension benefits going forward
but also backwards. The idea that the fund would be able to fund all of those benefits
was basically shattered in 2009.

Holtzman adds that the calculation is made on a cash basis rather than accrual basis:
the question is, if you stopped today how much of the liability could you pay off?
Ross notes that the consequence of a high unfunded liability is a higher cost for the
employer, rather than the employee, which is why you see the employer contribution
rates going up.

Molano asks: what has been the most impactful action that other Cities have taken to
improve their liability?
Holtzman answers that San Jose had a system where any excess earnings were placed
into a special fund that would then somehow lead to more benefits. Holtzman notes that
ending that fund was impactful.

Molano expressed concern that congress may increase or do away with the limit on the
level at which one gets taxed for social security, which is tied to the cap on pensionable
compensation for PEPRA employees. If congress increases the former, it may increase
the City’s pension obligation by raising the cap on pensionable compensation for
PEPRA employees.

  5
 Holtzman notes that he was involved in the PEPRA business on behalf of cities and was
upset that it didn’t do as much as he hoped it would have on prospective benefits for
current employees. He had hoped for higher employee cost shares, which can be
negotiated. Holtzman notes that the biggest changes to vested liability has been in
retiree health areas rather than pension, but retiree health runs by somewhat different
rules than pension. He adds that part of that is because there is a lot more local control
on retiree health.
Ross notes that the deferred compensation arguments relevant to pension are not
applicable to retiree health.

Holtzman notes there have also been attempts via ballot measure to change PERS, but
none have reached the ballot, in part because of the uncertainty in the law that Ross
described.

Holtzman notes that for the next meeting, either Bartel or his partner Mary Beth Redding
will present.

Wolfson notes that in the Rules of Order, it states that members are only allowed to
miss a certain number of meetings, and that the IBEW representative has not attended
a single meeting.

  5. REPORTS
  a. Brown Act Presentation from City Attorney

Garcia notes that he can give the Brown Act presentation first thing next meeting,
focusing on the issues regarding social media and serial meetings.

  6. REQUESTS FOR ITEMS ON FUTURE AGENDAS

Molano notes that he sent out materials that he would like the committee to see
regarding the Little Hoover Commission. Molano would like the group to read that
material prior to Bartel’s presentation.

Holtzman states that he will put that material in the reports section for the next session.

  7. ADJOURNMENT

Amirian motions to adjourn.
Wolfson seconds.

Meeting adjourns at 8:16pm.
